synopsis: Germany’s PEGASUS project is a substantial but narrowly scoped precedent: it ran from January 2016 to June 2019 for 42 months, involving 17 partners, about 1,791 person-months and EUR 34.5 million to define validation methods for a Level 3 highway chauffeur [f1204, f1285, f15693]. PEGASUS and VVM are cited as examples where reduced physical testing rested on years of prior simulation and statistical-tooling investment, although VVM and SET Level were not verified in the research and require checks before reliance [f1257, f4336]. BMW stated on 6 February 2026 that German authorities recognize virtual crash tests following a TÜV SÜD audit, but supplied no physical-test reduction percentage [f7566]. Germany also supplies relevant institutional and testing infrastructure through ASAM, DIN and CARISSMA, although the booklet does not cite DIN directly [f13222, f15030, f16122]. Important gaps and risks remain: German collision breakdowns by machine movement type were not found, and January 2026 Freshfields commentary says Germany’s draft implementing law presumes defect on non-disclosure regardless of fault [f3170, f10681].
